title: Practice Set PMSI1 — Reading the Executor
description: Mid recognition track: read the Spark UI Executors tab. Five signals at once — peak heap, GC time, task time, shuffle read, container kills — and decide which executor is in trouble. Companion to PSI8 (Memory Management) + PSI9 (Performance Monitoring).

tasks.title: Reading the Executors Page — One Tab, Five Signals

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer is investigating slow daily-billing pipeline runs. Senior asks them to open the Spark UI's Executors tab and walk through what they see. The cluster has 5 executors running a 12M-row sort-merge aggregation. The Executors page shows per-executor metrics. The engineer needs to interpret five signals at once and identify which executor is in trouble.
description.task: Which executor is in trouble, and what is the dominant signal?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Executor Count: 5

Executor Memory: 8g per executor

Stage: Sort-merge aggregation by region of 12M meter rows

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
Spark UI → Executors tab snapshot

Executor   Peak Heap   GC Time    Task Time   Shuffle Read   Container Kills
1          4.2 GB      18 sec     240 sec     580 MB         0
2          4.1 GB      22 sec     250 sec     590 MB         0
3          4.0 GB      19 sec     245 sec     575 MB         0
4          7.8 GB      220 sec    280 sec     6.2 GB         0
5          4.1 GB      20 sec     248 sec     590 MB         0

fields.label: Which executor is in trouble, and what is the dominant signal?
options: All five are healthy. Peak heap below 8 GB on all, no container kills, GC within tolerance. Executor 4's higher numbers reflect a slightly less-balanced shuffle but within Spark's tolerance band.
Executor 4. The 0 container kills is misleading — kills only register after the task finishes. The 7.8 GB peak heap and 220 sec GC are precursor signals to a kill that has not yet happened.
Executors 1, 2, 3, 5. Their ~4 GB peak on 8 GB heap suggests Spark's Tungsten allocator wastes 50% on alignment padding. Fix: enable spark.memory.offHeap.enabled to bypass alignment.
Executor 4. The dominant signal is GC Time at 220 sec — 79% of task time. The shuffle read of 6.2 GB (10× the others) fills the heap to 7.8 GB and forces constant GC. The root cause is data skew.
fields.correctAnswer: Executor 4. The dominant signal is GC Time at 220 sec — 79% of task time. The shuffle read of 6.2 GB (10× the others) fills the heap to 7.8 GB and forces constant GC. The root cause is data skew.
fields.rationale: Reading the Executors tab requires comparing rows.2 GB shuffle read (10×).
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats a 10× shuffle read imbalance as 'within tolerance'.Spark's tolerance band is roughly 2×; 10× is structural skew.

tasks.psReference: PSI8 lesson 3 (OOM Diagnosis from Executor Metrics), PSI9 lesson 4 (Reading the Executors Tab).

tasks.title: GC Time of 4 Minutes per Task — What Does It Mean?

description.context: Two NordGrid pipelines have similar runtimes but different GC profiles. Pipeline A's Spark UI shows 4 minutes of GC time on EVERY executor across all tasks. Pipeline B's Spark UI shows 4 minutes of GC time on ONE executor only. The senior engineer asks: same number, different shape — which is which problem?
description.task: Which pipeline has cluster-wide GC pressure and which has per-executor skew?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Task Count: 200

Executor Count: 5

Wall Clock: ~12 min on each pipeline

evidence.label: Pipeline A — Spark UI Executors tab
evidence.content:
Executor   Heap (peak / 8GB)   GC Time   Task Time   Shuffle Read
1          7.5 GB              240 sec   720 sec     1.2 GB
2          7.4 GB              225 sec   720 sec     1.2 GB
3          7.6 GB              250 sec   730 sec     1.2 GB
4          7.5 GB              235 sec   720 sec     1.2 GB
5          7.4 GB              240 sec   720 sec     1.2 GB

evidence.label: Pipeline B — Spark UI Executors tab
evidence.content:
Executor   Heap (peak / 8GB)   GC Time   Task Time   Shuffle Read
1          3.8 GB              18 sec    245 sec     590 MB
2          3.7 GB              22 sec    245 sec     580 MB
3          7.9 GB              240 sec   285 sec     6.0 GB
4          3.9 GB              20 sec    245 sec     595 MB
5          3.8 GB              19 sec    245 sec     585 MB

fields.label: Which pipeline has cluster-wide GC pressure and which has per-executor skew?
options: A is cluster-wide pressure (uniform high heap and GC across all workers). B is partition imbalance (only worker 3 elevated). The clue is whether GC is uniform or concentrated on one worker.
Both show cluster-wide GC pressure; the difference is just magnitude. A's 240 sec across 5 executors equals B's 240 sec on one — same total JVM cost. The same fix applies: raise --executor-memory.
B has cluster-wide pressure (the single executor at 240 sec drags the whole stage). A has per-executor skew (each executor has its own load profile, visible in heap and shuffle-read columns).
Neither has either condition; both show normal execution with GC within tolerance. The 240 sec is misleading because the column shows CUMULATIVE GC across the application, not per-task GC.
fields.correctAnswer: A is cluster-wide pressure (uniform high heap and GC across all workers). B is partition imbalance (only worker 3 elevated). The clue is whether GC is uniform or concentrated on one worker.
fields.rationale: The diagnostic question is where GC time is CONCENTRATED.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Sums GC time across executors.The shape (concentrated vs spread) carries the diagnostic, not the total.
Option C: Inverts the mapping.

tasks.psReference: PSI8 lesson 1 (Spark's Memory Architecture), PSI9 lesson 5 (Cluster-Wide vs Per-Executor Pressure).
